Looking at the redirect route, I notice it sends users to whatever URL was stored as the original link, which is only validated as a well-formed URL at creation time. Since anyone can create a shortened link pointing to any external destination, this is inherently an open redirect by design—the core feature of a URL shortener—but it's worth flagging since it could be abused for phishing with no additional safeguards in place.

I'm also noting the lack of rate limiting across the redirect route and server actions, which leaves the system open to enumeration, abuse, or resource exhaustion through mass link creation. Additionally, I want to check whether the URL validation restricts dangerous protocols like `javascript:`, `data:`, or `file:`, since a generic URL format check might not block these.

Confirming that Zod's z.url() accepts any protocol by default unless explicitly restricted, so javascript: URLs would pass validation - this is a real finding worth flagging, recommending restricting to http/https.

Other things to check: there's no rate limiting on the server actions for creating, updating, deleting links, which could allow abuse even though Clerk might offer some bot protection. Also looking at how short codes are generated using random bytes encoded as base64url, considering whether 48 bits of entropy is sufficient.

I'm verifying that updateLink and deleteLink properly scope queries by userId to prevent IDOR, while the short code uniqueness check is correctly global rather than per-user. I'm also confirming Next.js server actions have built-in origin checking that covers CSRF concerns, and that the dashboard renders URLs as text rather than through dangerouslySetInnerHTML, avoiding XSS. Now I'm moving on to inspect the middleware configuration.

Also checking the tmp/ folder for JSON files that might leak sensitive debug data, and reviewing next.config.ts for missing security headers like CSP, X-Frame-Options, or HSTS. I'll also look at .gitignore and the remaining component files (header, edit-link-dialog, delete-link-dialog) for any issues.

# Useful patterns

## SRI hash for CDN scripts
When adding CDN `<script>`/`<link>` tags, add `integrity` + `crossorigin="anonymous"`.
Don't trust scraped/fetched hash text (jsdelivr package pages are JS-rendered, hashes often missing from fetched text).
Compute reliably via PowerShell instead:
```
$client = New-Object System.Net.WebClient
$bytes = $client.DownloadData("<url>")
$hash = [System.Security.Cryptography.SHA384]::Create().ComputeHash($bytes)
"sha384-" + [Convert]::ToBase64String($hash)
```
Official docs (e.g. getbootstrap.com quickstart) also directly publish correct integrity hashes for their own CDN snippets - prefer those when available.

## Static HTML projects (no build step)
For "static html project" requests, use CDN-hosted libraries (Bootstrap, Chart.js, etc.) instead of npm/package.json - avoids requiring a build step.
